claims.claim: The unit-cost model permits arbitrary-length integer addition, subtraction, multiplication and floor division.
Remainders and the constants0,1,2 are constructed from permitted operations.
The equality-only test of positivity handles x=1 before dividing by x-1.
Packing nonnegative coefficients below A allows exact base-A coefficient extraction.
The chosen A exceeds every needed binomial coefficient throughout the factorial computation.
Repeated halving and squaring construct the initial binary scale in O(log n) permitted steps.
The invariant t=A^m,u=(A+1)^m,v=m! is preserved by doubling the binary prefix.
Extracting the central binomial coefficient converts (m!)^2 into (2m)!.
The optional next bit updates all three quantities with a constant number of steps.
The factorial algorithm uses a fixed number of registers and O(log n) unit operations.
The least h with n dividing h! satisfies gcd(h,n)>1.
For prime n, h=n; for composite n>4, h<=n-2.
The exceptional n=4 is handled by the preliminary gcd branch.
The power-of-two bracket b! nonzero and (2b)! zero modulo n is found in O(log n) steps.
A nontrivial gcd(n,b!) is proper because n does not divide b!.
When gcd(n,b!)=1, the central-binomial test is equivalent to factorial divisibility only on the stated interval.
The first successful central index is ceil(h/2) in(b/2,b].
The repaired Fibonacci initialization m=b-s brackets that index and initializes powers by exact division.
Extending the test to true beyond b preserves monotonicity without evaluating invalid binomial indices.
The simultaneous Fibonacci updates preserve the power invariants.
Both outcomes preserve m<z0<=min(m+s,b).
At s=1, the two final gcd candidates include the required factor and are proper for composite n.
Each Fibonacci stage has constant unit cost; the register count remains fixed.
C0176's n=35 transition violates the printed upper invariant after the known2002 correction.
That invariant counterexample alone is not asserted to be an incorrect final f(35) output.
The sum of logarithms across one factorization-tree level is at most log n.
Every branch has logarithmic depth, giving O((log n)^2) unit operations for complete factorization.
The packed registers may have O(n^2) bits; this is not a logarithmic bit-time algorithm.
The Robinson floor identity follows from the stated product and a tail error below1.

claims.claim: Every N-survivor up to N^3 is1, a prime, or a product of two primes greater than N.
This partition gives pi(N^3)=pi(N)+f(N^3,N)-1-f2(N^3,N).
Ordering the two primes counts each semiprime exactly once, including squares.
The number of partners for p is pi(N^3/p)-pi(p)+1.
Summing pi(p)-1 produces the displayed difference of two binomial coefficients.
All needed quotient arguments are below N^2.
The seven partner counts for N=10 are24,21,16,15,14,11,11 and give f2=63.
Dividing deleted multiples by the current prime proves the survivor recurrence.
Every recursion node has a squarefree product and a Mobius sign.
The ordinary leaves are exactly squarefree k<N and contribute mu(k)*floor(N^3/k).
The special leaves are exactly kp_j crossing N with all prime factors of k greater than p_j.
Their remaining sieve argument is p_(j-1), as in the known correction.
The strict and nonstrict leaf boundaries must be changed together; the printed convention is consistent.
For N=10 the ordinary sum is-9 and the signed special sum is-237.
Consequently f(1000,10)=228 and pi(1000)=168.
Sum-tree updates and prefixes require O(log N) operations.
The printed shifted leaf indexing is correct with a separately counted1 and the stated prefix length.
The elementary finite Euler-product bound gives a prime reciprocal sum O(log log N).
There are at most N*pi(N) special-leaf candidates.
The full time is O(N^2 log N log log N), with O(log N)-bit arithmetic quantities.
Precomputed least prime factors and Mobius values need O(N) words.
Each block's prefix totals are updated only after its queries at the current sieve level.
The exact k interval assigns each quotient query to one block.
These k intervals are disjoint across blocks for a fixed prime, avoiding an extra factor N.
Two coordinated segmented sieves also compute f2 in O(N) words.
The recorded time bound implies O(N^(2+epsilon)) for every fixed positive epsilon.
The O(x^(1/2+epsilon)) analytic prime-count method is an explicitly cited external theorem.
The exact pi(10^20) value agrees with the primary table.
The pi(10^23) table value is a later blue annotation, not an original2006 entry.
Platt reports a rigorous unconditional pi(10^24) computation; it was not rerun locally.
The2022 pi(10^29) value and attribution agree with the authors' record.
The2022 Hirsch-Kessler-Mendlovic addition is supported by its title and introduction, not an independent proof of the full paper.
The inverse rbar exists and gives nonzero unit residues rprime and u.
Every desired divisor and its complement correspond uniquely to nonnegative lambda,mu.
The product equation implies the displayed linear congruence modulo s.
Theta=ceil(sqrt(N/s)) gives the required product bound; the printed floor does not establish it.
The Euclidean vectors retain the congruence, alternating signs and determinant magnitude s.
The adjusted last exact quotient ends at(-s,0) and adds at most one Euclidean step.
A sign change on the nonpositive-coefficient subsequence produces the weighted small linear combination.
The intermediate positive-coefficient vector supplies the alternative bound2T.
The initial and final vectors include the zero-lambda and zero-mu boundaries.
All desired solutions lie in one enumerated congruence interval for z.
The substitutions A=v3*(lambda*s+r) and B=v1*(mu*s+rprime) have sum H and product v1*v3*N.
Solving the quadratic gives denominator2*v3*s for lambda and2*v1*s for mu.
The repaired formulas are reversible for nonnegative-square discriminant and positive integral lambda,mu.
C0177's printed denominator can output4 as a divisor of14.
C0178 is the false auxiliary floor bound; no general failure of the floor-only algorithm is claimed.
The enumeration may repeat a valid divisor, as acknowledged in the answer.
Each vector contributes O(1+Theta/s) candidate z values.
O(log s) Euclidean vectors give O(sqrt(ceil(N/s^3))*log s) arithmetic operations.
All intermediate bit lengths are O(log N), allowing constant multiples of that length.
Integer square root is explicitly counted as an arithmetic operation; its bit implementation has its own cost.
The original Lenstra algorithmic section supports the derivation and differs at the erroneous book denominator.
CRT gives (p+1)(q+1)/4 squares including zero and (p-1)(q-1)/4 unit squares.
Squaring is a permutation on each odd-order nonzero-square component and fixes zero.
Every square therefore has exactly one canonical square root in Q.
The m=209 examples satisfy the modulus and prime-interval assumptions inherited from3.5P.
The parity-negation identity needs nonzero tau; zero and nonunits have separate gcd branches.
Modular halving gives tau(v/2)=(tau(v)+m*lambda(v))/2.
The sum-parity identity follows by the integer carry multiple of odd m.
The unit Jacobi-positive class splits into disjoint Qstar and minus Qstar.
The sign chi is invariant under multiplication by4.
The canonical root of v^2*y is chi(v)*tau(v) on the nonzero-chi classes.
Uniform x has four preimages per unit square, two per nonzero nonunit square and one for zero.
Consequently the oracle promise on uniform Q does not imply the printed mean for x^4 samples.
The saved m=209 oracle succeeds on31/60 uniform squares but only93/209 of the x^4 sampling distribution.
For the printed majority size, that counterexample makes the correct answer probability below3*10^-7.
The repaired membership algorithm first handles zero, proper gcd and Jacobi-negative input.
Its sample size is ceil(8*epsilon^-2*log(2/delta)).
The nonunit-square proportion theta is at most four times the proper-gcd sampling probability rho.
If rho is large, the gcd branch succeeds with the required high probability.
If rho is small, the oracle retains a positive margin on uniform unit squares.
Conditional on all samples being units, the samples remain independent and uniform in the unit group.
The two Jacobi-positive sign classes produce opposite parity and the correct majority direction.
Hoeffding gives the stated error and O(epsilon^-2*log(2/delta)*(T(G)+r^2)) time.
A dyadic eta between epsilon/8 and epsilon/4 permits finite explicit grids.
Trial division up to B either factors m or makes both primes larger than every sample-index difference.
In the latter branch, nonunits have sufficiently small mass to preserve oracle bias on Qstar.
A Jacobi-negative x makes its canonical square root different from both x and minus x.
Recovering that root yields the two proper gcd factors.
Uniform a,b and their rare-zero events are analyzed without conditioning away pairwise independence.
All O(eta^-4) initial approximation/parity branches are enumerated, including the true one.
The simultaneous halving updates preserve and shrink both approximation errors.
The two linear sample families give uniform individual inputs and pairwise-independent pairs by invertible determinants.
The correct vote uses floor(alpha_t+j*beta_t+beta_(t+1)), not the printed product; C0182 has a valid local witness.
The numerical approximation error is uniformly bounded outside explicit endpoint bands.
The signed vote handles chi=-1 by flipping the predicted canonical-root parity.
The auxiliary error variable must use lambda(chi(u)*u); C0184's printed expectation fails even for a perfect oracle.
The corrected error variable depends only on its own multiplier and fresh oracle coins.
Its mean is at least eta and its variance at most1 under the recorded constants.
Chebyshev bounds each majority failure by1/(n_t*eta^2).
The union bound includes both votes at every stage starting at zero.
The printed C0185 bound omits stage zero; for r=8 its own stated terms sum to19/18.
That upper-bound arithmetic error does not establish actual failure probability above9/10.
Using ideal stage errors bounds the first actual error without invalid conditional independence assumptions.
Chi values are reused after two stages because the multipliers differ by a square.
The membership precomputation's errors have a separate union bound.
After r stages, nearest-integer recovery determines the exact tau value.
Each reconstructed branch must produce a proper gcd, not merely a root with the right square.
A trial succeeds with probability greater than one half, so expected repetition count is constant.
Fresh coins are kept for different oracle positions even when their numerical inputs coincide.
The short approximation precision and streamed recovered bits give the recorded word-operation bound.
The total time is O(r^2*(epsilon^-6+epsilon^-4*log(1/epsilon)*(T(G)+r^2))).
The stronger Fischlin-Schnorr Theorem8 is an explicit external input, unnecessary for the proved main construction.
The P4 composition uses predictor time T_bit=T(test)+O(N*R^2); substituting that cost gives the recorded bound.

The norm product uses x1*x2+a*y1*y2 in its first coordinate.
The inverse of a unit-norm pair is norm^-1 times(x,-y).
Multiplication by a fixed unit-norm pair bijects the two norm fibers.
The printed minus sign in C0169 fails for a=2 and the stated small pairs, including modulo5.
For split a there are p-1 solutions of each nonzero norm; for nonsplit a there are p+1.
Lifting gives the full product formula over prime powers.
C0172's minus branch modulo8 has the solution(2,1); only the plus branch demonstrates nonexistence.
The two-dimensional lattice has determinant magnitude |m|*sqrt(|a|).
Gauss reduction and the reduced angle bound give min Q<=|m|*sqrt(4|a|/3).
C0170 omits |m|; a=2,s=17,z=6 gives minimum2 above sqrt(8/3).
The norm quotient t is an integer and satisfies |t|<=sqrt(4|a|/3).
The explicit alpha pair has norm s*t and is nonzero.
The m=0 and a=0 degeneracies have direct constructions.
A shortest vector is primitive, allowing the zero-norm branch to find a root or proper gcd.
For a=1 the difference-of-squares formula solves the equation using invertibility of2.
For a=-1 the required progression modulo4n is a unit class and the sum-of-two-squares construction applies to its primes.
The nonzero-coordinate sampling in C0171 is not uniform across nonzero norms; n=7,a=3 supplies exact unequal counts.
Sampling both coordinates over all residues makes unit norms conditionally uniform by the fiber count.
The proper-gcd, zero-norm and nonunit-coordinate branches must be adjusted with that sampling change.
The distribution counterexample alone does not prove that the original method is inefficient.
The centered representative satisfies |a|<=n/2.
A found modular square root is checked directly before using it.
For s=1 the sampled pair inverse already gives the answer.
The gcd of m or t with n either splits the problem or permits the required inverse.
For t=0, primitiveness supplies a root of a or a proper factor.
The recursive solution X^2-tY^2=a either gives a factor, a square root, or an invertible Y.
The pair beta=(X/Y,1/Y) has norm t with respect to the original a.
Composing alpha*beta^-1*(u,v)^-1 has norm b.
The square-root shrinkage gives O(log log n) coefficient levels down to plus or minus1.
A discovered divisor and its quotient are not assumed coprime.
Repeated gcd stripping separates the prime supports into coprime components.
The joint derivative gcd allows lifting even if neither derivative coefficient is separately invertible.
Repeated squaring of the lifting modulus has polynomial bit length and reaches the required component.
The recursive component products are bounded by n and CRT recombination is valid.

claims.claim: Each smooth power gives a whole exponent-vector relation modulo p-1.
One common integer combination of rows must produce each coordinate basis vector.
The logarithm of a factor-base prime uses the original power exponents r_i in that combination.
C0173's p=7,a=3 example returns1 instead of the correct logarithm2.
Independent coordinate coefficients do not give a simultaneous row combination.
The modulus p-1 is composite, so an arbitrary nonzero pivot cannot be inverted.
The Bezout two-row transform is unimodular and preserves the full integer lattice.
Reducing rows above the positive pivots bounds intermediate bit lengths polynomially.
Index one yields every unit basis vector and its explicit coefficient certificate.
Membership tests allow redundant relation rows to be discarded without factoring p-1.
A proper subgroup has a nonzero prime-order linear character vanishing on it.
Choose a factor-base coordinate with nonzero character coefficient.
Pair each small smooth v with q_j*v; at least one exponent vector is outside that subgroup.
Every smooth integer occurs at most twice as an endpoint, giving the stated lower count.
Random exponents give exactly uniform nonzero residues because a is primitive.
Every trial enlarges a proper subgroup with the recorded conditional probability, for any prior history.
Each enlargement at least doubles subgroup size, bounding their number by d*log2(p-1).
A central binomial coefficient divides the lcm up to2m, yielding an elementary lower bound for psi.
Subtracting repeated prime powers gives pi(x)>=c*x/log x for large x.
Products of k distinct factor-base primes give binom(d,k) distinct bounded smooth integers.
The chosen B and k yield Psi>=exp(log p-O(sqrt(log p*log log p))).
The expected relation collection and integer elimination cost is exp(O(sqrt(log p*log log p))).
The proof uses no unproved smoothness hypothesis or random-matrix rank assumption.
Markov converts the expectation into the required almost-always p^epsilon cutoff guarantee.
The shifted target b*a^r is uniform and has the same smoothness lower bound.
Its factorization yields the target logarithm modulo p-1 after subtracting r.
The representative0 is returned as p-1 under the book's exponent convention.
A final power check validates the output.
The known1998 final-modulus correction is incorporated and is not C0173.
The original Adleman article is source support; our full-factor-base proof covers the different book implementation.
The improved constant in the Coppersmith-Odlyzko-Schroeppel abstract is explicitly heuristic and is not used in our unconditional bound.
The bit-mask dot product in equation17 is the stated binary parity.
Setting the mask to1 gives the simple BBS least-significant-bit rule.
Squaring permutes the unit quadratic residues for the stated distinct Blum primes.
The3.5F and4.5.4-43 reductions now provide the requested forward cross-reference.
The modulus distribution must be the same in the random source and in the factoring average.
The reductions are conditional implications and do not prove hardness of factoring.
